questions.q: What does the Pauli X operator do to a qubit, and what is it the quantum analog of?
options: It flips only the relative sign between |0⟩ and |1⟩ without changing measurement probabilities
It permanently destroys the qubit's quantum state
It swaps |0⟩ and |1⟩ (X|0⟩=|1⟩, X|1⟩=|0⟩), making it the quantum analog of a classical bit flip
It leaves the qubit completely unchanged
questions.explain: X|0⟩=|1⟩ and X|1⟩=|0⟩ -- it swaps the basis states exactly the way a classical bit flip swaps 0 and 1, which is why X is called the bit-flip operator.

questions.q: Why is a Pauli Z (phase-flip) error invisible to a measurement made directly in the computational basis?
options: Because Z always converts |0⟩ into |1⟩, identically to X

Z leaves |0⟩ and |1⟩ individually unchanged except for a sign on |1⟩ (Z|0⟩=|0⟩, Z|1⟩=−|1⟩), so the probabilities of measuring |0⟩ or |1⟩ are identical before and after -- the sign only matters for interference, not direct computational-basis readout
Because measurement itself is physically incapable of detecting any kind of quantum error
Because Z errors never actually occur in real hardware
questions.explain: Z(α|0⟩+β|1⟩) = α|0⟩−β|1⟩ -- measuring in the computational basis gives |α|² and |β|² either way, so the sign flip is undetectable without measuring in a different basis (such as the |+⟩/|−⟩ basis).

questions.q: In the |+⟩ = (|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2, |−⟩ = (|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2 basis, what does the Z operator do, and why does this explain the name 'phase-flip'?
options: Z swaps |+⟩ and |−⟩ (Z|+⟩=|−⟩, Z|−⟩=|+⟩), the same role X plays in the {|0⟩,|1⟩} basis -- so Z is a bit-flip with respect to the phase-defining |+⟩/|−⟩ basis, which is exactly the 'phase' being flipped
Z leaves |+⟩ and |−⟩ completely unaffected, proving Z has no measurable effect in any basis
Z only acts on |+⟩ and |−⟩ states if the qubit has already undergone an X error first
Z converts |+⟩ into |0⟩ directly, bypassing the |−⟩ state entirely
questions.explain: Z|+⟩=|−⟩ and Z|−⟩=|+⟩ mirrors how X|0⟩=|1⟩ and X|1⟩=|0⟩ behave in the computational basis -- Z is literally a bit-flip operator for the +/- basis, which is the relative-phase basis, hence 'phase-flip'.

questions.q: How does the Pauli Y operator relate to X and Z?
options: Y is a completely independent fourth error type unrelated to X or Z in any way
Y is simply another name for the identity operator (no error at all)
Y only ever occurs in multi-qubit systems and never affects a single isolated qubit
Y is equivalent, up to an overall phase factor of i, to applying X and Z together (Y = iXZ) -- physically, a Y error is a simultaneous bit-flip and phase-flip on the same qubit
questions.explain: Y = iXZ, so up to a global phase, a Y error is X and Z occurring together -- this is why error-correcting codes designed to catch X and Z independently also catch Y automatically, as their simultaneous occurrence.

questions.q: Why does the lesson emphasize that essentially any single-qubit error can be decomposed into a combination of the identity, X, Y, and Z?
options: Because it means only X errors ever occur in real quantum hardware
Because it proves that quantum errors are actually impossible to correct in practice

Because it means engineers don't need a different correction scheme for every physically distinct noise source -- a code built to detect and correct X and Z (and therefore Y) can in principle correct any single-qubit error, regardless of its underlying physical cause
Because it shows that classical and quantum error correction use identical mathematical techniques with no differences
questions.explain: This decomposition is the conceptual foundation of quantum error correction: however messy the real physical noise process is, its effect reduces to some combination of I, X, Y, Z, so correcting X and Z (which also catches Y) is sufficient in principle -- exactly what the bit-flip and phase-flip codes in Chapter 3 are each built around.
